Chapter 4: The Power of Strengths—Identifying and Using Core Virtues.
Here’s something fascinating about positive psychology. Real, lasting fulfillment doesn’t come from obsessing over what’s wrong with us. Instead, it comes from recognizing and leaning into our own strengths. Think of these strengths as the psychological version of muscles. The more you exercise them, the more energy, confidence, and genuine satisfaction you’ll feel.
And here’s the thing—strengths aren’t just about talents or flashy skills. They’re also about character. Traits like kindness, curiosity, perseverance, and gratitude. Each of us has a unique mix of these virtues, shaped by our upbringing, our culture, and our life stories. The trick is to figure out which strengths feel most natural and energizing to you, and then start using them more often.
Discovering your strengths is a little like searching for hidden treasure. Sometimes, they’re right on the surface—maybe you’re someone who just naturally connects with others, or maybe you love diving into new ideas. Other times, you’ll need to reflect on your proudest moments or past successes. Ask yourself questions like, “When do I feel most alive?” or “What do people often thank me for?” You might be surprised at what comes up.
Once you’ve spotted a few of your core strengths, the next step is weaving them into your daily life. And you don’t have to overhaul everything—small, practical steps are enough to make a difference.
For instance, you could pick just one strength to focus on each week. Then, look for fresh situations to use it—at work, at home, even with friends. Take a moment every day to notice how using this strength shifts your mood, your energy, or even your relationships.
Let’s say creativity is one of your top strengths. Maybe you find new ways to tackle everyday problems or bring a fresh perspective to your team. Or, if fairness matters most to you, you might volunteer for roles where impartial judgment really counts.
The amazing part? Using your strengths doesn’t just boost your own satisfaction. It has a ripple effect. When you act from your best qualities, you’re more engaged, more resilient, and even more generous with others. This creates a kind of positive feedback loop—your well-being grows and, before you know it, it spreads through the people around you.
Here’s something to keep in mind: strengths aren’t set in stone. Just like with physical fitness, you can train and develop them over time. Set goals, ask for honest feedback, and reflect on your progress. That’s how you build new strengths and make your existing ones even stronger.
So, what’s the real takeaway? The road to true happiness is lined with the recognition and use of your own strengths. When you focus on what’s best in you, instead of what’s missing, you’ll find a sense of fulfillment that’s not only real, but sustainable.
